title: Vaulting mechanics successfully predict decrease in walk-run transition speed with incline
population: Humans walking on the level and up a 9.8% incline (sample size not stated in the abstract); compass-gait model
findings: A compass-gait vaulting model extended to inclines agrees with earlier observations that walk-run transition speed falls approximately 1% per 1% incline.
Measured preferred walk-run transition speed lay below the predicted maximum walking speed.
Actual maximum walking speeds were above predictions.
Onset of compliant walking on level and incline occurred near predicted values.
Preferred absolute transition speeds may be influenced by additional factors.
limitations: Theory plus a small laboratory experiment (the abstract does not give the sample size); one incline measured (9.8%); walking speeds at the transition, not hiking at ultra durations or in fatigued runners. The measured preferred transition lay consistently below the predicted maximum walking speed.
implications: A gradient-dependent walk/run switch is plausible: transition speed falls approximately 1% per 1% incline (from earlier observations, matched by the vaulting model), so on steeper grades walking becomes the natural gait at progressively lower speeds.
Use only as a prior; the paper states that preferred absolute transition speeds may be influenced by additional factors.

verification.notes: Crossref: Biol Lett 9(2):20121121, 2013, two authors match. PubMed PMID 23325739 abstract checked. The 1% per 1% figure is the earlier observation that the model reproduces, not a new measurement. Sample size unstated in abstract.
